summary: Gives the IAB's evaluation of the present and near-term effects of CIDR on organizations using classful routing technology. It is informational and now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet changed how it hands out addresses. This memo warns old equipment owners what the change means for them.

questions: how does cidr affect classful routing
what did the iab say about cidr
subtitle: How CIDR affected networks using older address technology

tldr.problem: The Internet was transitioning from classful routing (where addresses came in fixed-size classes) to CIDR (classless routing with variable-size blocks). Organizations with older routing equipment that did not support CIDR needed to understand how this change affected them.
tldr.mechanism: CIDR-capable routing protocols like OSPF, RIP II, IS-IS, and BGP-4 can aggregate routes using variable-length subnet masks. Older protocols like RIP, BGP-3, and EGP cannot. Organizations stuck with old routing technology must rely on default routes, potentially resulting in suboptimal routing paths.
tldr.outcome: The IAB evaluated the implications and effectively warned organizations that they would need to upgrade to CIDR-capable routing to remain part of the main Internet. Sites unable to upgrade would fall back to using default routes and accept worse routing performance.

today: RFC 1817 is Historic. By the 2000s, CIDR had become the standard for all Internet routing. Classful routing technology is obsolete and no longer used in production networks. IPv6, the next-generation protocol, uses CIDR-like addressing from its inception. This RFC is retained as a historical record of how the Internet managed one of its most significant architectural transitions.

sections.title: The CIDR Transition
sections.content:
CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) fundamentally changed how the Internet assigns and routes IP addresses. In the old classful system, addresses came in three fixed-size classes: Class A networks (16 million addresses each), Class B networks (65,536 addresses each), and Class C networks (256 addresses each). An organization got one whole class, no matter if it needed only a fraction of that space.

CIDR eliminated classes and instead allows addresses to be allocated in blocks of any size. A small organization can get exactly 512 addresses; a large one can get 65,536. This efficient allocation, combined with route aggregation (grouping multiple networks into one routing table entry), reduced the explosive growth of routing tables that was threatening the Internet's scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way: you get a whole huge block of addresses whether you needed them or not. CIDR: you get only what you actually need, and routers can group them together in the routing table.

sections.title: CIDR-Capable vs. Classful Routing
sections.content:
To use CIDR effectively, interior routing protocols (those used within an organization) must support Variable Length Subnet Masks (VLSM). The protocols that support CIDR are OSPF, RIP II, Integrated IS-IS, and EIGRP. The exterior protocol that supports CIDR is BGP-4 (Border Gateway Protocol version 4).

Older protocols do not support CIDR. RIP (the original version), BGP-3, EGP, and IGRP cannot understand the variable-size address blocks that CIDR uses. These protocols were designed when classes existed, and they still assume class-based addressing.

An organization operating as an Internet Service Provider (ISP) must support CIDR-capable routing to participate fully in the Internet. However, smaller sites that rely on a single default route for external connectivity may not strictly require CIDR support internally, though they lose some routing efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: New protocols understand CIDR and can be smart about routing. Old protocols do not understand it. If you have old equipment, you have to fall back to a default route and accept worse performance.

sections.title: Implications for Organizations
sections.content:
The IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) was beginning to allocate IP addresses from what had been the Class A address space (64.0.0.0 through 126.0.0.0) in variable-sized blocks based on actual organizational requirements. Sites receiving these addresses were required to support CIDR-capable routing.

For organizations using old classful routing technology, there were two choices: upgrade to CIDR-capable routing protocols, or continue using default routes and accept suboptimal routing. A default route sends all traffic destined for unknown networks to a single gateway, which may result in inefficient paths compared to the optimal route. Organizations hoping to avoid this suboptimality would need to transition to CIDR-capable protocols like OSPF or BGP-4.

The memo effectively served as notice that the Internet's architecture was changing, and organizations needed to prepare for the transition or accept degraded performance.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want good routing, you have to upgrade your equipment to understand CIDR. If you do not, your traffic will take longer paths, but you can still use the Internet.
